a.statement: In a sorted array, find two numbers that add up to a target using O(1) extra space.

b.statement: In an unsorted array, find two numbers that add up to a target and return their original indices.

items.difference: Sorted order lets two pointers decide which end to move, in O(1) space. Unsorted data has no order to exploit, so you look up each complement in a hash map: O(n) space, but no sort and the original indices are kept.
rubric: Sorted versus unsorted is the deciding detail.
Two pointers rely on order to know which pointer to move.
The hash map trades O(n) space for not needing order.

a.statement: All numbers are positive. Find the longest contiguous subarray whose sum is at most k.

b.statement: Numbers may be negative. Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k.

items.difference: With only positives, growing the window raises the sum and shrinking lowers it, so a window knows when to shrink. Negatives break that, so you count earlier prefix sums equal to current − k with a hash map.
rubric: Negative numbers are the deciding detail.
A window needs the sum to move predictably as it grows or shrinks.
Prefix sums with a hash map handle any sign.

a.statement: Find the fewest moves from the start of a maze to its exit.

b.statement: Count how many separate open regions a maze has.

items.difference: Fewest moves needs BFS, which reaches cells in order of distance. Counting regions only needs to explore each region once, in any order, so DFS (or BFS) from each unvisited cell works.
rubric: "Fewest" asks for distance, which needs BFS.
Counting regions is connected components: any full search works.
DFS can find a long path first, so it isn't safe for shortest paths.

a.statement: Attend as many non-overlapping meetings as possible.

b.statement: Make an amount with the fewest coins, where the coins are 1, 3 and 4.

items.difference: For meetings, always taking the one that ends earliest is provably safe, so greedy works. For coins 1, 3 and 4, the biggest-coin choice can be wrong (6 = 4 + 1 + 1 versus 3 + 3), so you must compare options with DP.
rubric: Greedy works only when a local choice is provably safe.
A counter-example (6 with coins 1, 3, 4) shows greedy fails for coins.
DP considers every choice using stored sub-answers.

a.statement: List every combination of the given numbers that adds up to the target.

b.statement: Count how many combinations of the given numbers add up to the target.

items.difference: Listing them means generating each one, which is exponential and needs backtracking. Counting only needs the number of ways for each smaller target, which overlap, so DP gets it in about O(target × numbers).
rubric: "List every" means you must produce each combination: backtracking.
"Count" only needs a number per subproblem: DP.
Counting can be far faster than listing.

a.statement: Find the longest substring without repeating characters.

b.statement: Find the length of the longest common subsequence of two strings.

items.difference: A substring is contiguous, so a sliding window can grow and shrink over it. A subsequence can skip letters, and matching two strings creates overlapping subproblems over their prefixes: a 2D DP table.
rubric: Substring means contiguous; subsequence can skip.
Contiguous runs suit a sliding window.
Subsequences of two strings need a DP table over prefixes.

a.statement: For each day, find how many days until a warmer one.

b.statement: Find the k hottest days of the year.

items.difference: The next warmer day depends on position: the nearest greater item to the right, which a monotonic stack finds in O(n). The k hottest overall ignores position, so a heap of size k keeps the best k in O(n log k).
rubric: "Next warmer" is about position: a monotonic stack.
"k hottest" ignores position: a heap.
Both are about larger values, which is why they look alike.

a.statement: Decide whether a linked list contains a cycle.

b.statement: Decide whether a set of course prerequisites contains a cycle.

items.difference: Each linked-list node has one next pointer, so fast and slow pointers detect a loop in O(1) space. Prerequisites form a general directed graph with many edges per node, so you need a graph search, such as Kahn's algorithm or DFS with on-path tracking.
rubric: A linked list has one outgoing pointer per node.
Prerequisites form a general directed graph.
Graph cycle detection needs a visited set or in-degrees, not two pointers.

a.statement: Find the maximum depth of a binary tree.

b.statement: In a huge, lopsided binary tree, find the depth of the shallowest leaf.

items.difference: Maximum depth needs every path, so a recursive traversal combining both subtrees is natural. The shallowest leaf is found level by level, so BFS can stop at the first leaf it meets without exploring the deep side.
rubric: Max depth needs every node anyway: recursion.
The shallowest leaf favours level order.
BFS can stop early; DFS might explore a deep branch first.
